Palash Interiors: Three Numbers on a Sunday Night

Bengaluru, Sunday 14 June 2026. Three feature proposals, three impact estimates adding to ₹424 crore, an engineering budget of ₹11 crore, and a suspicion that none of the three numbers means what it appears to mean.

1. Sunday night, Sadashivanagar

The rain had come early that year. Arundhati Deshmukh — Aru to everyone at Palash Interiors, including the two co-founders — had spread three printed one-pagers on the dining table of her flat in Sadashivanagar at about seven in the evening, intending to finish by nine. It was now twenty past eleven. Her son had been put to bed, her husband had given up and gone to watch the second half of a football match, and the three one-pagers had been joined by a fourth sheet, unprinted, on which she had been writing the same three sentences over and over in different arrangements.

At ten the next morning the capital allocation committee would meet in the glass room on the fourth floor of the Domlur office. Vikram Sathe, the chief executive, would chair it. Meghna Iyer would fly in from Mumbai. Rohan Kulkarni would join from Pune on video, Lena Hoffmann from Berlin at six-thirty in the morning her time, Dr Sandhya Raghavan from Toronto at half past midnight hers because she had insisted. The committee would allocate the FY27 product and engineering budget: ₹11 crore of build capacity, which at Palash's blended cost translated to roughly forty-two engineer-quarters, against three proposals whose stated first-year impacts, if you simply added them, came to ₹424 crore of additional booked project value on a base of ₹612 crore.

Aru had written all three impact estimates herself, or had signed off on them, which amounted to the same thing. She had believed them when she wrote them. What had changed over the weekend was not any single fact but the accumulation of small ones: a line in a designer-capacity spreadsheet that Arun Menon had sent on Friday without comment; a footnote in Sandhya's model documentation that she had read properly for the first time; and a conversation on Saturday morning with a customer in Whitefield who had explained, patiently and at length, why she had walked away from a Palash quote for reasons that appeared in none of the three proposals.

The uncomfortable thought, the one Aru kept writing and crossing out, was this: the three numbers were not wrong in the way a badly built spreadsheet is wrong. They were wrong in the way a map of the wrong city is wrong.

2. How Palash was built

Palash Interiors was founded in Bengaluru in 2018 by Vikram Sathe, formerly of a furniture retail chain, and Priyanka Sathe, an architect, on a thesis that the Indian home-interiors market — then estimated at something over ₹2 lakh crore a year and almost entirely unorganised — would consolidate around whoever could make a full-home interior project predictable in price and time. The customer was a family taking possession of a two- or three-bedroom apartment in a new tower, with a budget somewhere between ₹6 lakh and ₹22 lakh, a possession date they did not control, and a deep fear of the local carpenter-contractor who disappears for eleven days in the middle of a kitchen installation.

By FY26 Palash operated in nine cities, ran fourteen experience centres, worked with 1,430 registered interior designers, booked ₹612 crore of project value, recognised ₹487 crore of revenue on execution, and lost ₹71 crore. The average booked project value was ₹8.4 lakh. Bookings ran at roughly 610 a month.

One decision from 2021 shaped everything that followed. Faced with the cost of employing designers in nine cities and the impossibility of forecasting demand across festive and possession cycles, the founders converted the design function into what the company called the Design Partner Network. Designers were no longer employees. They were independent partners who signed a standard agreement, used Palash's quoting and project tools, and earned a share of project value — between 7 and 11 per cent depending on tier — with no retainer. The model worked: gross margin improved by nine percentage points in eighteen months, and the company survived the 2022 funding winter when two competitors did not.

It also fixed two things in place that Aru could not now move. First, clause 6.3 of the partner agreement guaranteed each partner a minimum number of assigned leads per month in exchange for exclusivity of their working hours — which meant lead routing was not a free optimisation problem but a contractual allocation. Second, because partners were not employees, Palash could not direct their schedules. It could not simply ask the network to take 30 per cent more consultations next quarter. It could only recruit more partners, which took eleven weeks from application to first project, and which the current tier structure made unattractive in exactly the cities with the most demand.

3. The market around it

By mid-2026 the organised end of Indian home interiors had four recognisable kinds of competitor. Livspace and HomeLane had both matured into large, multi-city, capital-heavy platforms with their own factories. Design Cafe had held a strong position in the South. IKEA's Indian stores and its online catalogue had, since Bengaluru and Mumbai opened, reset what customers believed a wardrobe should cost, and the Asian Paints Beautiful Homes service had brought a trusted national brand into the full-home category with a distribution advantage no startup could match. Below all of them sat Pepperfry, Urban Ladder and an ocean of local contractors who quoted on WhatsApp and worked for cash.

Three structural forces bore directly on Palash's funnel. The first was possession timing. The single strongest predictor of a booking was the gap between the enquiry and the customer's apartment possession date; RERA registration data, published state by state, made project-level possession schedules partly visible, and builders in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad and the Mumbai Metropolitan Region increasingly ran their own handover-day interior fairs. The second was GST: modular furniture attracted 18 per cent, and the tax line on a ₹9 lakh quote was a real objection that local contractors, quoting without invoices, did not have to answer. The third was credit. Home-improvement lending had grown quickly through NBFCs and through bank offerings, and the Reserve Bank's digital lending guidelines — key fact statements, restrictions on default loss guarantee arrangements, rules on who may originate — determined exactly how a platform like Palash could present an EMI option inside its own quote flow. Payments ran through Razorpay; the 10 per cent booking token was almost always paid by UPI.

Palash's global exposure was smaller than its org chart suggested but disproportionately profitable. Farida Qureshi's team in Dubai worked with Sufouh Realty, a brokerage serving non-resident Indian buyers, and had originated 214 projects in FY26 at an average value of ₹19.6 lakh — more than twice the domestic average, paid in full up front, and requiring remote handover. Dinesh Varadhan, in Edison, New Jersey, ran a similar motion into the US-based NRI market, smaller and slower. Together the two channels were 4 per cent of bookings and 11 per cent of gross profit.

4. The situation, in sequence

October 2025. The board approved an FY27 plan built on taking bookings from 610 a month to 1,000 a month by March 2027. Nobody in the room disputed that the lead volume existed; the debate was entirely about conversion.

November 2025. The growth team changed the definition of a lead. Until then a lead was a completed form on the website or app. From 1 November it also included any inbound WhatsApp enquiry that reached the business number, because Meta's click-to-WhatsApp campaigns had become the cheapest source of volume. Monthly leads jumped from about 41,000 to about 62,000 in six weeks. Every ratio with leads in the denominator fell correspondingly, and Exhibit 1 carries the scar.

January 2026. Sneha Pillai, a growth product manager, ran a four-week pilot in Pune matching enquiries against RERA possession schedules and sending a staged WhatsApp nurture sequence timed to possession minus ninety days. The pilot cohort booked at 1.9 per cent against 1.1 per cent for the rest of Pune. Sneha wrote the second of the three proposals on the strength of it.

February 2026. Rohan Kulkarni's team in Pune shipped a stripped-down version of a self-serve room configurator to web traffic in Bengaluru only, as a three-week test. Exhibit 4 reports the result. The test is the evidential basis for the largest of the three estimates.

March 2026. Meghna Iyer opened discussions with two NBFCs about an embedded finance option presented at the moment a quote is issued. A term sheet exists. It is not signed.

April 2026. Arun Menon's delivery organisation reported that consultation slots in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune were running at 91 per cent of available partner capacity on weekends, when 78 per cent of consultations happen. The report went into the weekly operations pack. Aru read the summary line, not the annexure.

22 May 2026. Sandhya Raghavan's team delivered the impact model that converts a claimed step-level lift into annualised booked value. Aru's three proposals all use its output. Its documentation contains a paragraph, under the heading Assumptions and limits, stating that the model treats each funnel stage as having unconstrained capacity and that estimated lifts above roughly 8 per cent at any stage should be read as upper bounds. Aru read that paragraph on Saturday.

6 June 2026. Farida Qureshi wrote from Dubai to say that Sufouh Realty had asked whether Palash could guarantee a fixed price for a full-home project agreed remotely, because two of its clients had been quoted one figure in February and invoiced 14 per cent more in May. Nobody had connected this to the configurator proposal, which is, in effect, a promise of an instant price.

5. The people

Arundhati Deshmukh, 39, Vice-President Product, Bengaluru. Joined in 2022 from a payments company. She owns the funnel and she owns the three estimates. Her stated position is that the committee should fund one feature properly rather than three thinly. Her incentive is that her own performance is measured against the 1,000-bookings-a-month plan she helped write. What she is not saying is that she now believes the plan is not achievable through any product change at all, and that saying so on Monday would be read as walking away from her own number four months after signing it.

Vikram Sathe, 47, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. He wants the instant configurator. His stated reason is customer experience: he tells the story of his sister-in-law waiting eleven days for a quote. His incentive is a Series D conversation with two funds who have both asked, in different words, what Palash has that Livspace and HomeLane do not. What he is not saying is that one of the two funds explicitly mentioned a self-serve product experience as a condition of interest, and that he has already described the configurator to them as being in development.

Meghna Iyer, 44, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. She wants the embedded finance option, which she frames as the only proposal that improves unit economics rather than volume: a lending partner would pay a subvention of 2.2 to 3 per cent of project value. Her incentive is a cash runway of nineteen months. What she is not saying is that the NBFC term sheet assumes Palash takes a first-loss position that the Reserve Bank's guidelines would constrain, and that her finance team has not yet obtained a legal opinion on the structure.

Rohan Kulkarni, 41, Director of Engineering, Pune. His stated position is that the configurator is three quarters of work, not the two quarters in the proposal, because the pricing engine cannot currently produce a quote without a site measurement. His incentive is delivery credibility. What he is not saying is that three of his eight senior engineers have offers from a Pune-based SaaS company and that a three-quarter project with a public commitment attached is his best argument for retaining them.

Lena Hoffmann, 36, Design Director, Berlin. She has worked on European furniture configurators and is the only person in the company who has watched one fail. Her stated position is that an instant price which is later revised destroys more trust than a slow price. Her incentive is the integrity of the design experience she has spent two years building. What she is not saying is that she has been interviewing, and that her view of the Indian market is formed largely from Bengaluru and Mumbai customer calls conducted in English.

Dr Sandhya Raghavan, 43, Head of Data Science, Toronto. She built the impact model. Her stated position is that the committee should fund the cheapest proposal and instrument it heavily. Her incentive is that her model's credibility is about to be tested in public. What she is not saying is that her team excluded 24 per cent of exposed sessions from the February configurator test as bot-like, that the exclusion rule was written after seeing the data, and that the effect size is not robust to including them.

Arun Menon, 50, Head of Design Delivery, Hyderabad. His stated position is that the funnel does not have a conversion problem above the consultation, it has a capacity problem at it. His incentive is partner satisfaction, which is measured monthly and which falls when partners are given more leads than they can serve. What he is not saying is that his own partner-recruitment target for FY26 was missed by 31 per cent and that a capacity narrative conveniently explains a growth shortfall he was accountable for.

Sneha Pillai, 29, Growth Product Manager, Bengaluru. She wrote the possession-date nurture proposal and ran the Pune pilot. Her stated position is that her proposal is the cheapest and the most certain. Her incentive is her first large mandate. What she is not saying is that the Pune pilot cohort was hand-selected by a city manager who chose enquiries from four premium builder projects, and that she has not been able to reproduce the match rate against RERA data outside Maharashtra.

Farida Qureshi, 38, Head of NRI Partnerships, Dubai. She wants remote price certainty for Sufouh Realty's clients. Her incentive is a channel whose margin protects her headcount. What she is not saying is that two of her recent projects were re-quoted upward after site measurement and that she absorbed the difference out of her channel budget rather than escalate.

The only number that moved is the denominator, and it moved because a definition changed. A reader who starts at the left of the table sees a collapsing funnel. Exhibit 3. What last year's estimates turned out to be worth

Aru had asked for Exhibit 3 in April, and had been slightly sorry she did. The pattern in it is not random error. The four features that over-estimated were all screen-level changes whose estimates were built by multiplying a step conversion rate by a total population. The one that under-estimated was a change to how quickly a human being called a customer back. Whatever the impact model is measuring, it measures the second kind of change badly and the first kind of change generously.

Exhibit 6. The capacity ceiling

Exhibit 6 is the sheet Arun Menon sent on Friday without comment. Against 4,890 consultations attended in May there were, on this construction, 5,180 available. The headroom in the whole network is 290 consultations a month, and it sits in Kochi and Jaipur while the demand sits in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune. If Proposal A delivers the 18 per cent lift in consultations booked that Exhibit 4 promises, it books 1,415 additional consultations a month into a network with room for 290 of them, most of them in the wrong cities. Read this way, Exhibits 4 and 6 are not two views of the same funnel. They are a claim and its refutation, and they have been circulating in the same company for two months without anyone putting them on the same page.

7. Voices

“I am not asking for a perfect number. I am asking for a number I can say out loud to a fund without being embarrassed in eighteen months. Give me the configurator number.”

Vikram Sathe, executive review, 4 June 2026

“We have built a machine that turns any product idea into a two-hundred-crore number. That is not a compliment to the machine.”

Dr Sandhya Raghavan, in the #fy27-planning channel, 9 June, 11:47 p.m. IST

“Aru, please look at the annexure and not the summary. My partners in Bengaluru are declining leads. Declining. In a market where they earn only when they close. Ask yourself what that means before you send them 1,400 more.”

Arun Menon, email, Friday 12 June, 6:10 p.m.

“In Hamburg we shipped a configurator that gave a price in ninety seconds. The revision rate after measurement was thirty-one per cent. Customers do not experience a revised price as new information. They experience it as the first price having been a lie.”

Lena Hoffmann, design review, 2 June 2026

“Two of Sufouh's clients were quoted in February and invoiced fourteen per cent higher in May. I have taken that on my budget twice. I cannot take it a third time and I cannot sell price certainty we do not have.”

“The subvention is two point two per cent of project value on every financed booking. At forty per cent penetration that is nine crore a year of margin that does not depend on us converting one extra customer. Why is this even a debate?”

“My builder handed over in March. Your designer came on the twenty-second. By then I had already signed with a fellow my neighbour used, because he came on the fourteenth. Your price was better. He was there first.”

8. The options as Aru currently frames them

The one-pagers on the dining table present the decision as a choice among three builds, and Aru has spent the weekend working inside that frame because it is the frame the committee expects.

Option one: fund Proposal A. Build the instant configurator, accept Rohan's three quarters, spend ₹4.7 crore and roughly two-thirds of the FY27 capacity, and tell the Series D funds a story about self-serve. The estimate of ₹210 crore rests on Exhibit 4's step lift surviving all the way to a booking, which Exhibit 4 itself does not show, and on capacity existing to serve the consultations it generates, which Exhibit 6 says does not exist. In its favour: it is the only proposal that changes what Palash is, rather than how efficiently it does what it already does.

Option two: fund Proposal B. Spend ₹1.2 crore on possession-date targeting, mostly in Maharashtra where the RERA match rate is 81 per cent, and treat the other cities as a data-acquisition problem to be solved by builder partnerships rather than by scraping. The estimate of ₹120 crore is almost certainly too high by the argument of Exhibit 5, but the underlying capability — knowing which enquiries are ninety days from possession — would also let Palash route the scarce consultation slots of Exhibit 6 to the enquiries most likely to use them. That second effect appears in no proposal and in no estimate.

Option three: fund Proposal C. Ship embedded finance, take Meghna's subvention, and accept that the ₹94 crore is a volume story layered on a margin story that stands on its own. This is the only proposal whose value does not depend on the funnel moving at all. It is also the only one with a regulator in it, an unsigned term sheet, and a legal question nobody has answered.

What the frame excludes is everything that Arun Menon and the Whitefield customer were pointing at. Nothing on the table adds consultation capacity, changes how leads are allocated under clause 6.3, or shortens the twenty-two days between enquiry and a designer standing in a customer's flat. Those are not features, so they did not generate one-pagers, so they have no impact estimates, so they will not be on the wall on Monday. The three numbers Aru is about to defend are all answers to the question how much more of the funnel could we convert, and it is not obvious, at half past eleven on Sunday night, that this is the question.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee meets at ten on Monday 15 June and will not meet again before 4 September, because Vikram leaves for a three-week investor trip on 1 July and Meghna's audit closes in August. Whatever is funded on Monday defines the engineering roadmap to March 2027.

The constraints are these. Cash: nineteen months of runway at the current burn, or fourteen if the FY27 hiring plan is executed in full. Capacity: ₹11 crore, about forty-two engineer-quarters, of which eight are already committed to a GST invoicing rework that cannot be deferred. People: Rohan's three senior engineers, and a partner network whose Bengaluru tier-one designers are turning leads down. Contract: clause 6.3, which guarantees lead minimums to partners and which cannot be amended without renegotiating 1,430 agreements. Regulation: the Reserve Bank's digital lending framework, which shapes what Proposal C may look like and who may hold first loss; the DPDP Act, which governs whether RERA-derived possession data may be joined to enquiry records and used to message people who have not consented to that use; and GST at 18 per cent on modular work, which no product change will remove. Market: Livspace and HomeLane are both running aggressive possession-season campaigns in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, and Asian Paints' Beautiful Homes has opened two new studios within four kilometres of Palash's Indiranagar experience centre.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Reconstruct the three impact estimates in Exhibit 2 on a common base. What does each proposal claim once the populations, the overlaps and the November lead-definition change in Exhibit 1 are reconciled?

2. Exhibit 4 shows a lift at one step that disappears at the next. List the explanations consistent with the data, and say for each what evidence would distinguish it — and whether that evidence can be gathered before Monday, before September, or at all.

3. Exhibit 3 shows a median estimate-to-realised ratio of 3.1 times, with the two closest estimates attached to operational rather than screen changes. What does that pattern imply about how Palash should construct and discount its estimates? What would you change in the method rather than in any one number?

4. Exhibits 4 and 6 cannot both be acted on naively. If the binding constraint is consultation capacity rather than consultation demand, how does that change the value of each of the three proposals — and what fourth proposal does it imply that nobody has written?

5. Each of the eight stakeholders has an incentive that shapes the number they brought. Design a process for FY28 planning that would surface those incentives without making the exercise adversarial. What does Aru lose by introducing it, and who would resist?

6. It is ten o'clock on Monday morning. What does Aru actually say in the first three minutes, what does she recommend the committee fund, and what does she tell the board in September if the number she defends on Monday turns out to be wrong by a factor of three?

Sunday night, continued

At a quarter past midnight Aru put the three one-pagers into a folder and did not put the fourth sheet in with them. On it she had written, in the end, only two lines. The first was the funnel has not got worse; it has not got better either, and we changed the denominator so we could not tell. The second was a question rather than a statement: if we had 290 spare consultations a month and one crore, what would we spend it on?

She did not know whether that was the insight that would save Monday or a way of avoiding the meeting she was actually going to have. Vikram had already told two funds about the configurator. Meghna had a term sheet with a date on it. Rohan had three engineers who needed a reason to stay. Arun had a capacity number that made his own missed target someone else's problem, and was, in all likelihood, correct anyway. Sandhya had a model whose limits she had written down in a paragraph that nobody read, including Aru, until this weekend. Somewhere in Whitefield a customer had signed with a carpenter who came eight days earlier and charged more.

The rain had stopped. Aru switched off the dining-room light and left the folder on the table, where she would see it at six.

Estimating Feature Impact

A near-expert treatment: what the arithmetic hides, where the schools of thought part company, and how the number behaves once an organisation starts believing it.

I. Two rooms, ten days apart

On Tuesday 4 February 2026, in a glass-walled room off Bengaluru's Bannerghatta Road, Aparna Deshmukh had eleven proposals and three engineering pods. She was group product manager for origination at Chandrika Credit, a digital lender with 22 lakh monthly actives and roughly 8.4 lakh loan applications started every month. The allocation meeting was in nine days. Her chief risk officer had told her, without much warmth, that two proposals touched the mandatory know-your-customer sequence, and that nothing in that sequence could be removed, only re-ordered. Her chief financial officer wanted every proposal expressed as incremental contribution rather than gross disbursal, because the previous year the roadmap's stated impact had summed to more than the company's entire annual growth.

Aparna's problem was not method. She had run impact estimates for six years and could produce one in an afternoon. Her problem was that her team's last four estimates had, on measurement, delivered between a fifth and a half of what they promised, and everyone in the room knew it. The number had stopped functioning as evidence and started functioning as advocacy.

Ten days later and four hundred kilometres south, on Thursday 12 February, Siddharth Nene faced a structurally different version of the same question. He was director of product at Tarakendra Systems, a Chennai company selling warehouse-execution software to large Indian retailers and third-party logistics operators: 62 enterprise accounts, ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, top-five concentration of 41 percent. His board wanted him to choose between a labour-forecasting module and a yard-management module, and to justify the choice with a number. Siddharth had no funnel worth the name — only 62 accounts with named commercial owners, and a sales cycle in which one conversation with the supply-chain head at Brihaspati Retail, an account worth ₹14.2 crore of ARR on its own, mattered more than any percentage point.

Both were sizing what a change could do before building it. What separates a competent practitioner from an expert is visible in how differently these two problems must be handled, and in how much of the standard method silently assumes Aparna's world and breaks in Siddharth's.

II. The idea, its history, and the people who disagree about it

An impact estimate is a decomposition. It expresses the expected change in a business metric as a product of separately-reasoned factors — how many units of demand pass through the affected stage, what fraction are eligible, what fraction of those encounter and adopt the change, how much the adopting group's behaviour shifts, and what one unit of shifted behaviour is worth — attaching uncertainty to each factor rather than to the product alone. Every term is a claim someone can be wrong about in an identifiable way, and that localisation of error is the point. An intuitive guess of ₹20 crore can only be right or wrong; a decomposition can be wrong in the eligibility term, which is something you can go and check on Wednesday.

The lineage predates product management. Enrico Fermi's habit of decomposing unknowable quantities into knowable-enough factors gave the family its name, and Frank Drake's 1961 equation its canonical public form. Decision analysis in the 1960s, through Ronald Howard and Howard Raiffa, added the machinery product practice still mostly ignores: explicit distributions over inputs, sensitivity analysis to find which input drives the decision, and the expected value of information, which asks what it is worth to reduce uncertainty in that input before committing. Douglas Hubbard's calibration work added the finding that untrained estimators are badly overconfident. Product management absorbed a thin version of all this in the 2010s through ICE and RICE, which made the decomposition popular while stripping out the distributions that made it honest.

Four positions are worth separating, because practitioners routinely argue past each other by conflating them.

The decomposition school would sign: a structured estimate with stated assumptions is superior to expert intuition even when both are wrong, because it tells you where the error lives and who should go check it. It would not sign: the resulting point estimate is a usable forecast of what will happen.

The empiricist school, built on the large experiment portfolios documented by Ronny Kohavi and colleagues — in which roughly a third of well-reasoned ideas move the metric, a third do nothing and a third do harm — would sign: the only trustworthy estimate of an effect is a randomised measurement of it, and pre-build estimates are biased upward by a factor of two to five. It would not sign: therefore do not estimate.

The portfolio school, closer to venture thinking, would sign: the purpose of estimating is rank-ordering and variance-shaping, not accuracy; a roadmap whose items all have well-estimated modest returns is a badly constructed portfolio. It would not sign: every proposal must clear a numerical return threshold, because that rule eliminates exactly the unestimable bets that produce most of the upside.

The counterfactual school, out of causal inference and pricing, would sign: an impact number is meaningless without an explicit statement of the world in which you do not build it. It would not sign: last quarter's observed rate is the counterfactual.

Aparna's organisation had run the decomposition school's arithmetic while making the portfolio school's promises and ignoring the counterfactual school's warnings — an ordinary combination, and why her last four estimates missed.

III. Mechanics in depth: the chain, and the terms that leak

The chain experts build has more links than the two-step version taught to beginners. For Aparna's leading proposal — pre-filling the KYC form from an account-aggregator consent instead of asking the applicant to re-key identity and bank details — reach is 8.4 lakh applications a month; eligibility, the share whose banks are live on that network, is 54 percent; encounter-and-adopt, from a painted-door test, is 65 percent of the eligible. The effect term holds most of the judgement, and it is not a percentage-point figure at all. It is a proportional reduction in the drop-off: the KYC step converted at 71 percent, so 29 percent leaked there, and the hypothesis was that pre-fill removes 30 percent of that leak — 8.7 points, for adopters only. Diluted to the whole population, 0.54 × 0.65 × 8.7 = 3.05 points.

The rest is mechanical: 8.4 lakh × 3.05 percent = 25,620 additional completions a month; 46 percent reach disbursal, giving 11,785 loans; at ₹1,480 of net contribution each — ₹42,000 average ticket, after cost of funds, expected credit loss and servicing — that is ₹1.74 crore a month, ₹20.9 crore a year, less a 25 percent deferral haircut for applicants who would have completed on a second attempt anyway: ₹15.7 crore.

Three things there separate expert from competent practice, and none are arithmetic.

Estimating on the leak rather than the rate. A step converting at 71 percent and one at 92 percent cannot both gain "three points" from a similar intervention; the second has only eight points of failure to work with. Experts reason in proportional reduction of the remaining friction, which behaves sensibly near the ceiling. The same 30 percent relative improvement yields 8.7 points at the first step and 2.4 at the second.

Dilution applied inside the chain, not to the conclusion. The 8.7 points is an effect on adopters; what an experiment reported over all applicants shows is 3.05, because only 35.1 percent are triggered. Teams that estimate the triggered effect and measure the overall one find a discrepancy of exactly the trigger share and conclude the feature underperformed, when estimate and measurement were answering different questions.

Checking that the estimate is measurable before promising to measure it. The sample-size approximation for a difference in proportions at eighty percent power and five percent significance is n ≈ 16·p(1−p)/Δ² per arm. At p = 0.71 and Δ = 0.0305 that is about 3,540 per arm — days of traffic. Had the diluted effect been 0.3 points, it would have been 366,000 per arm, a month of total volume split two ways. The estimate thus tells you not only what to expect but whether you will ever be allowed to know.

The formal treatment of uncertainty is most often skipped and most changes behaviour. If each factor in a five-term chain carries an honest ninety-percent range spanning a factor of two — a log standard deviation of ln(2)/(2 × 1.645) ≈ 0.21 — and errors are independent, the product's is 0.21 × √5 ≈ 0.47, so its ninety-percent range spans exp(2 × 1.645 × 0.47) ≈ 4.7 times: here, roughly ₹7 crore to ₹33 crore. That is not a failure of the method but the method telling the truth. A ±20 percent band around a five-term product is not more precise, only less honest.

This is the practical residue of expected value of information, and the habit that most visibly marks an expert: refine what could change the answer, leave the rest rough.

IV. When the method applies, stated as claims you can test

Four conditions carry most of the weight, and each is checkable.

Claim one: the metric decomposes into stages whose baseline rates are stable. The test is the coefficient of variation of each stage rate across eight to twelve recent weeks, excluding campaigns. Chandrika's KYC completion rate moved within 69 to 73 percent across a quarter — stable enough that a three-point prediction means something. Tarakendra's equivalent, the share of pilots converting to paid rollouts, swung between 20 and 60 percent depending on which three accounts were in the pipeline: for Siddharth the rate is not a property of the system but an average over a few idiosyncratic negotiations.

Claim two: the effect is local to one or two stages. KYC pre-fill touches one step and does not change who applies; a change to Chandrika's credit policy would move approvals, disbursal, ticket size and loss rate at once and in opposing directions, and no funnel decomposition would survive it.

Claim three: at least one anchor exists for the effect term — an internal measured launch, an external published result, or a cheap in-product probe such as a painted door. Aparna had the third, which is why she could defend 30 percent rather than assert it. Siddharth had none, and said so.

Claim four: the value of one unit of behaviour is knowable within a factor of two. True for a loan with a known contribution margin, roughly true for an enterprise seat, false for a trust or safety feature whose value is a reduced probability of a fat-tailed loss.

Where the method actively misleads, the failure is bias rather than noise. It misleads when the category does not yet exist, so the decomposition quietly assumes today's demand curve; for insurance-shaped work — fraud, compliance, reliability — where expected value is dominated by the tail; and most corrosively when the estimate becomes a target, since a team that has promised three points will find three points, by dark patterns or by re-instrumenting the funnel.

V. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the arithmetic is sound and the aggregation is not. When Chandrika's loans, cards and insurance teams each estimated against the same 22 lakh monthly actives, the three roadmaps summed to a growth rate the company had never achieved, because each counted the same attention twice. Only one of the two common fixes works: a metrics council that deduplicates populations and applies a haircut calibrated from past realisation rates, rather than a blanket finance discount, which teaches every product manager to inflate by the reciprocal within two quarters.

Two-sided businesses break the chain differently: a feature that lifts buyer conversion cannot deliver more than supply can serve, so the honest estimate is the minimum of the two sides. Rohini Marketplace, a home-services platform Aparna had worked at earlier, once estimated a booking-flow improvement at 14 percent and delivered four — in six of nine cities the roster was already at weekend capacity, so extra demand raised the rejection rate, which depressed repeat rate and turned a positive estimate slightly negative.

Regulated products cap the effect term from above: Aparna could not estimate removing a KYC step, only re-ordering it, so the ceiling was set by the regulator's mandatory sequence rather than by design quality. Hardware-plus-software businesses turn reach from a number into a curve. At Aakashganga Networks, a telecom-equipment maker Siddharth had advised, a firmware feature reached only the install base that had taken the quarterly update — 18 percent at ninety days, 61 percent at a year — so the first-year estimate was an integral over a ramp, not a multiplication.

AI-native products break two terms at once. At Grahan Labs, which sold an autonomous support agent to Indian consumer brands, the effect of any improvement depended on the resolution quality of a model replaced every few months, giving every estimate a shelf life of weeks; and the value term carried a variable inference cost that grew with adoption, so a wildly successful feature could be worth less per unit than a moderate one.

VI. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. Adopter lift is not causal lift

The commonest anchor compares users who used a feature with users who did not, and it is almost always badly inflated, because adopters self-select on intent. The tell is an analog phrased as "customers who used X converted 30 percent better." The obvious reading is wrong: the people who found X were already the likeliest to convert. The expert's reflex is to ask for both groups' pre-period behaviour — when Chandrika matched adopters and non-adopters on prior attempts and credit band, a 22-point gap collapsed to six.

2. Deferred conversions are not incremental conversions

Removing friction often moves a conversion forward in time rather than creating one. The tell is a weekly metric that lifts convincingly while the monthly cohort total stays flat. The obvious reading is that something else offset the gain; the correct one is that the unit of value is the cohort, not the week — which is why Aparna's binding constraint was a sixty-day window rather than traffic.

3. Novelty decay means the first reading is the wrong one

Effects measured in the first fortnight overstate steady state for anything that changes an interface, because existing users notice the change itself. The tell is an anchor sourced from a two-week readout, and the obvious reading ignores that the population later regresses partway. Experts ask for the week-six figure or state a decay assumption; novelty effects typically retain half to two-thirds of the initial lift, though friction removal decays far less than a new placement.

4. Dilution belongs in the estimate, not in the excuse

Triggered and reported effects differ by the trigger share, and the gap can be five-fold. The tell is a post-launch conversation in which someone says the experiment was diluted. The obvious reading is that measurement was unfair; the correct one is that the estimate was stated on the wrong population. Experts give both numbers up front and name which the readout will show.

5. The value term should be marginal contribution, not gross flow

GMV, disbursal and booking value are the denominators of choice for people who want a big number, and the tell is a set of business cases all applying the same take rate regardless of what they touch. The reading that revenue proxies value fails when features differ in variable cost: extra loan volume among thin-file applicants carries a different credit-loss provision than the same volume among repeat borrowers, and the difference can exceed the whole estimated gain.

6. Wide ranges are a sign of competence, not weakness

The multiplicative widening shown earlier means a five-term estimate honestly carries a several-fold range. The tell is a range narrower than any single input's uncertainty, and the obvious reading — that a tight range shows the analyst did the work — is backwards. The expert move is to present the range and then narrow the conversation to the one or two terms that drive it, which restores decisiveness without faking precision.

7. The counterfactual drifts

Impact is measured against a world in which you do not build, and that world is not static. The tell is an estimate using last quarter's level as the do-nothing baseline in a market growing four percent a month. The baseline looks like a fact but is itself a forecast, often the shakiest in the chain; holdouts exist precisely because the counterfactual must be observed rather than assumed.

8. The real deliverable is the assumption register, not the number

An estimate that lives only in a slide dies at the meeting, and the tell is that nobody can say, three months later, what it assumed. Experts leave a document listing each assumption, its source, a named owner and a reconciliation date — the mechanism by which an organisation's estimates get better rather than merely louder.

VII. How this changes across product types and stages

The arithmetic does not change anywhere; the chain is the same chain. What changes is where uncertainty concentrates and which term is knowable at all. In high-volume consumer products the population terms are precise, the effect term dominates uncertainty, and because measurement is cheap, accuracy matters less than rank order. In B2B and enterprise the position inverts: the effect on a given account is often confidently known by the account team, while the population is a handful of named logos whose behaviour is not statistically summarisable. Siddharth's estimate was therefore a scenario table rather than a mean, because the expected value of a two-moded distribution — Brihaspati Retail expands, or it does not — describes a world that will not occur.

Marketplaces add the binding-constraint rule: estimate both sides, take the minimum, and check the constrained side's rejection behaviour for knock-on effects on retention. Hardware converts reach into a ramp; AI products convert value into a margin with an expiry date. Where the differences are overstated, say so plainly: the claim that enterprise software cannot be estimated is false — it estimates well per account — and so is the claim that consumer products need more precision, since cheap measurement makes precision less valuable, not more.

Stage changes the purpose rather than the method. At seed stage an estimate exists to force explicitness, and ten-fold ranges are appropriate. At growth stage, with pods scarce and roadmaps contested, it becomes an allocation instrument and realisation tracking should begin. At maturity it becomes a budget instrument with political weight — precisely when independent review, deduplicated populations and calibrated haircuts stop being bureaucracy and start being the only thing keeping the numbers connected to reality.

VIII. Three worked examples, including one that failed

One: Chandrika Credit's KYC pre-fill. The chain in Figure 1 gave a base case of ₹15.7 crore with an honest range of ₹7 crore to ₹33 crore. The decision-relevant question was whether the low end cleared the opportunity cost of a pod for a quarter, about ₹4 crore. It did comfortably: the estimate was decisive despite being imprecise, and much energy is wasted narrowing ranges that were never going to change an answer.

Two: Tarakendra's module choice. Exhibit 2 gave labour forecasting ₹3.75 crore against yard management's ₹2.10 crore, built the same way. But 61 percent of that number rested on 18 accounts expanding at a rate Siddharth had assumed rather than observed, and ₹1.48 crore was churn protection, real but unmeasurable in any given year. He wrote both facts into the estimate rather than under it, and proposed a cheaper test: a paid pilot for four of the 18 accounts, converting an unfalsifiable assumption into an observable one within a quarter.

Three: the failure. Eight months earlier Chandrika had shipped a pre-approved-offer banner, estimated at ₹42 crore of annual contribution on the strength of an internal analog in which users who tapped a similar banner converted to disbursal at 31 percent against a 9 percent baseline. Measured against a five percent holdout kept running for ninety days, the realised figure was ₹6.1 crore. The post-mortem decomposed the miss into three multiplicative errors rather than one disappointment: matched analysis showed only 6 of the 22 raw points were causal, a factor of 0.27; about 30 percent of the remainder was deferred rather than incremental, 0.70; and an eligibility rule interacting with a caching defect meant the banner rendered in only 72 percent of intended sessions, 0.72. Multiplied, 42 × 0.27 × 0.70 × 0.72 ≈ ₹5.7 crore — nearly all of the observed result.

The recovery was procedural, not analytical. Any anchor from an unmatched adopter comparison now carried a mandatory 0.3 multiplier unless someone did the matching; every estimate had to name the population the launch would be read out on; and realisation ratios were logged. Across eleven launches the median moved from 0.38 to 0.76 — achieved mostly by estimating lower, the uncomfortable shape most genuine improvement in this discipline takes.

IX. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Each failure is cheap to detect at estimation time and expensive after launch, and the detection is a question rather than an analysis. That asymmetry is the case for reviewing estimates at all: fifteen minutes on the six questions in Exhibit 3 catches most of what a quarter of engineering would otherwise reveal.

X. Where experts genuinely disagree

Estimate first, or build a thin slice and measure? The empiricist position, steelmanned, is that estimation accuracy is so poor — realisation ratios of 0.3 to 0.5, success rates near one in three — that effort spent perfecting a projection is better spent making measurement cheap, and a two-week probe with a real holdout beats any amount of arithmetic. The evidence comes from very large experiment portfolios. It would be wrong where build costs are lumpy or irreversible — hardware, regulated flows carrying an audit burden, enterprise software where you cannot show half a module to Brihaspati Retail — and wrong in organisations whose constraint is decision quality rather than engineering throughput.

Should estimates be scored against outcomes? The calibration position holds that estimation is trainable only with feedback, and Chandrika's move from 0.38 to 0.76 is its evidence. The opposing position is that individually scored estimates produce sandbagging within two cycles: product managers learn to promise 60 percent of what they believe, preserving accuracy while destroying rank order, the only property that actually allocates pods. It would be wrong if scoring runs at portfolio level and sets a shared haircut rather than evaluating individuals — which is what Chandrika did, and possibly why it worked.

Does strategic value belong inside the number or beside it? One camp monetises option, defensive and platform value so they compete on equal terms, noting that whatever sits outside the number is systematically underfunded. The other holds that such terms are unfalsifiable and become the refuge of any proposal that cannot justify itself. The evidence is thin both ways; most mature companies run two lists with separately protected capacity, which nobody defends in principle and most find works.

XI. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. They estimate to a decision rather than to a number, asking first what threshold would change the choice and stopping once the answer sits clearly on one side of it. They spend effort asymmetrically, chasing only the terms the sensitivity table implicates. They state the estimate so it can be checked — the population the launch will be read out on, the window that separates deferred from incremental, the reconciliation date — making it the first half of a measurement rather than the whole of an argument. And they are comfortable saying a range is wide, knowing the alternative is not a better estimate but a more confident one.

XII. The decisions, and three questions

Aparna funded KYC pre-fill, on the ground that its pessimistic case exceeded the pod's opportunity cost and its two load-bearing assumptions were checkable within sixty days of shipping. She presented no point estimate: ₹7 crore to ₹33 crore, leak reduction and deferral named as the terms that mattered, a ninety-day holdout, and an assumption register with two named owners and a July reconciliation date. Siddharth chose neither module. He funded a four-account paid pilot of labour forecasting, reasoning that his estimate's entire spread lay in an expansion assumption he could buy information about for a fraction of the build cost — a decision his board first read as indecision and later called the most disciplined thing the product team did that year.

Three questions are worth sitting with. First: in your own most recent estimate, what threshold would have changed the decision, and how much of your analytical effort went to terms that could not cross it? Second: if your organisation's realisation ratio were logged and published, what would the median be, and which of the six failures in Exhibit 3 would explain most of the gap? Third: Chandrika Credit improved by estimating lower — under what circumstances is a systematically conservative estimator worse for a company than an accurate one, and who in your organisation would notice the difference?

XIII. Going deeper

  1. Fermi estimation — the parent discipline; practising it on verifiable quantities calibrates the judgement every term depends on.
  2. Constructing a funnel — unstable or overlapping stage definitions make every downstream estimate uninterpretable.
  3. Reading drop-off — teaches estimating on the leak rather than the rate, the largest correction on this page.
  4. Defining activation (the aha moment) — the one stage whose improvement compounds, and so the case a one-off estimate most understates.
  5. Cohort analysis — the machinery for separating deferred conversions from incremental ones.
  6. Retention curves and the PMF signal — where estimates must switch from per-event value to discounted lifetime value.
  7. Stickiness and natural frequency — sets the cohort window measurement needs before an estimate can be checked.
  8. Feature adoption analysis — supplies the encounter-and-adopt term empirically rather than by assumption.
  9. PM interviews — graders look for the decomposition and the sensitivity, not the answer.

Estimating Feature Impact

I. A number by Thursday

On the second Monday of March 2025, Ananya Bhatt, senior product manager for checkout at Kayaas Mart, a Pune-headquartered quick-commerce grocery app operating in forty Indian cities, had one engineering pod free for a six-week build and two candidate features competing for it. The first was a one-tap checkout that would remember a shopper's address and payment method so they never re-entered an OTP. The second was a "save for later" list that let shoppers park items from an abandoned cart and return to them without rebuilding the order from scratch. Both had obvious appeal. Neither had a number attached to it.

Her VP of product had been clear at the Monday stand-up: he did not want opinions on Thursday, he wanted a projection — expressed in orders and rupees, with a stated range and a stated confidence — for what each feature would do to checkout conversion over the following year. Kayaas Mart's checkout page saw roughly 480,000 carts opened every week; of those, 60 percent, or 288,000, became completed orders. A single percentage point of movement on that conversion rate was worth real money at the company's scale, and a badly reasoned percentage point pitched with confidence was worth nothing at all. Ananya's task was not to build either feature. It was to estimate, before either was built, which one was worth building — using nothing but the funnel numbers she already had and a set of assumptions she would have to state out loud in the room.

II. What an impact estimate actually is

An impact estimate is a structured Fermi estimate built on top of a funnel: it decomposes a proposed change into a handful of separately reasoned inputs — how many users the change touches, how much their behaviour would plausibly shift, and what that shift is worth — and multiplies those inputs back together into a defensible range, before anyone commits engineering time to building the thing well enough to measure it properly. It borrows its logic directly from Fermi estimation, the technique physicist Enrico Fermi used to teach students to guess the number of piano tuners in Chicago by breaking an unknowable quantity into knowable-enough pieces. Product teams adapted the same habit of mind during the 2010s growth-hacking era, when companies scaling fast — Facebook's growth team, then Sean Ellis's growth consultancies, then Intercom's public write-up of its RICE framework in 2016 — needed a repeatable way to compare feature ideas without a dedicated data scientist modelling every one. The problem it solves is specific: when engineering capacity is scarce and every proposal sounds plausible in a room, an organisation either builds everything it can imagine, which is impossible, or it lets the most senior or most persuasive voice decide, which is unaccountable. An impact estimate gives the room a number that can be argued with on its own terms. The sentence Ananya could repeat without sounding glib: an impact estimate decomposes the metric you care about into inputs you can reason about one at a time, and multiplies them back up into a range you would still defend after someone pokes at each assumption.

III. How the estimate is built

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and the steps practitioners skip are usually the ones that matter most. First, name the exact funnel stage the feature touches — not "checkout" in general, but the specific conversion rate between two adjacent, measurable states, here cart-opened to order-placed. Second, and this is the step most often left implicit, define reach: how many users per week actually pass through that stage and could in principle be affected, drawn from a stable baseline period rather than an unusually high or low week. Third, separately define affected population — the subset of that reach whose behaviour the feature could plausibly change, which is very often smaller than the full reach, because a feature aimed at friction only touches the users who experience that friction. Fourth, estimate the effect size: how much would the conversion probability shift for that affected population, stated as a percentage-point delta and sourced from something concrete — a similar feature shipped internally, a comparable one described publicly by a peer company, or a smaller pilot. Fifth, multiply reach (or affected population, whichever is correct) by the effect size to get a volume of additional conversions, and multiply that by the value of one conversion to get a rupee figure. Sixth — and this is the step teams most often skip under time pressure — build a low, base and high version of the whole calculation by varying the one or two inputs that are genuinely uncertain, rather than presenting a single confident point. Seventh, sanity-check the resulting number against the size of the whole business: if a single six-week feature implies double-digit percentage growth in company revenue, the estimate is almost certainly wrong, not the business.

IV. Running the numbers

Ananya modelled the one-tap checkout feature first. Her working hypothesis, drawn from a one-tap UPI autopay feature that Andaaz Wallet — Kayaas Mart's in-house payments arm — had shipped in the third quarter of 2024, was that removing repeated address and OTP entry would lift checkout conversion by three percentage points, from 60 percent to 63 percent, echoing the 2.4 points Andaaz Wallet had measured in a controlled test of its own. Applied naively to the entire weekly reach of 480,000 cart-openers, the arithmetic was: 480,000 × 0.03 = 14,400 additional completed orders per week; 14,400 × ₹640 average order value = ₹92.16 lakh in additional weekly GMV; annualised across 52 weeks, ₹47.92 crore in additional GMV; and at Kayaas Mart's roughly 20 percent net take rate across commission and delivery fees, about ₹9.58 crore in additional net revenue over a year. It was a striking number, and it was also, on inspection, wrong in an important way.

Her engineering lead pointed out that returning shoppers within the same month already had their address and payment method cached by the app's own remember-me cookie — the friction the feature removed simply did not exist for them. Only first-time-this-month checkout sessions, about 22 percent of weekly cart-openers, or 105,600 users, actually experienced the friction the feature was built to remove. Re-running the identical calculation on that corrected population — 105,600 × 0.03 = 3,168 additional orders per week; 3,168 × ₹640 = ₹20.28 lakh in additional weekly GMV; annualised, ₹10.54 crore in GMV; at a 20 percent take rate, roughly ₹2.11 crore in additional annual net revenue — cut the projection by more than three-quarters without changing a single arithmetic operation, only the definition of who was actually affected.

The direction of the recommendation survived; its magnitude did not. That gap — a live question about who is actually reached, not a dispute about the underlying effect size — is exactly the kind of thing a Thursday review exists to surface, and exactly the kind of thing a single, confidently delivered number hides.

V. What a learner has to become aware of

Reach is not the same as affected

The single most common source of an inflated estimate is applying an effect size to everyone who sees a screen rather than to the narrower group whose behaviour the change could plausibly alter. Kayaas Mart's own recalculation shows the gap can be a factor of four or more.

An effect size needs a source, not a hunch

"Three percent felt right" is not an estimate; it is a guess wearing an estimate's clothes. A defensible effect size traces back to an analogous launch — internal where possible, since context, audience and market maturity travel less well than people assume across companies.

The range is the point, not the hedge

A single number invites a yes-or-no argument. A stated low-base-high range tells the room which assumption to interrogate and how much is riding on it, which is the actual purpose of bringing the estimate to a meeting at all.

It says nothing about feasibility or cost

A large impact estimate does not mean a feature is cheap, safe, or technically simple to build in six weeks; it is one input into a prioritisation score, never the whole decision.

It does not know about interaction effects

If marketing launches a checkout discount the same quarter, the observed lift after shipping will blend both causes, and the pre-build estimate cannot separate them in advance; it can only flag that the risk exists.

It is easily confused with a business case

A business case weighs strategic fit, risk and opportunity cost alongside impact. An impact estimate answers a narrower question — what could this do to the funnel — and should be labelled as such rather than dressed up as the full argument for building something.

It suits near-term, funnel-adjacent behaviour, not brand or trust

Features that compound value over years — trust, habit, platform lock-in — resist this machinery, because there is no clean weekly funnel stage to decompose; those bets need a different kind of reasoning, closer to option value than to arithmetic.

The right question is always "what would flip the recommendation"

Before trusting any estimate, a newcomer should ask which single input, if wrong by half, would change the decision — and go find evidence for that input specifically, rather than polishing the parts that were already solid.

VI. Where the arithmetic changes

In a high-volume consumer product like Kayaas Mart, estimates lean on large populations and small percentage-point shifts, because the funnel is short, the traffic is heavy, and daily data accumulates fast enough to trust a two-week baseline. In a B2B product with forty enterprise accounts and a sales-assisted funnel, the same logic runs per account rather than per percentage point: a PM there estimates how many named accounts would plausibly renew a larger contract or expand seats, because the population is small enough to reason about individually rather than statistically. In a marketplace, a single-sided funnel estimate is not enough, because a feature that lifts buyer conversion can simultaneously suppress the supply side — a one-tap checkout that speeds buyers through might, for instance, reduce the browsing time that surfaces long-tail sellers — so a marketplace estimate has to model both sides and check that the net effect, not just the buyer-side effect, is positive. Company stage matters too: an early-stage team with thin historical data leans on external analogs and qualitative signals, accepting wider ranges as honest rather than sloppy, while a mature company like Kayaas Mart can draw on its own library of past launches — the Andaaz Wallet result Ananya cited being exactly that kind of internal analog — producing tighter, more defensible ranges because the comparison is closer to home.

VII. Where estimates go wrong

The first common mistake is stacking optimistic assumptions until the total conveniently matches what a favoured feature needs to look worth building; the symptom is a number that happens to clear the bar exactly, and the diagnostic is removing any single assumption to see whether the conclusion survives — if it does not, the estimate was reverse-engineered, not reasoned forward. The second is applying an effect size to the entire top-of-funnel population rather than the actual stage the feature touches, which is what Ananya's engineering lead caught; the tell is an implied growth rate the company has never once achieved, and the diagnostic is comparing the projected annual impact to the business's actual historical growth. The third is presenting a single point estimate with unearned confidence instead of a range, which turns a prioritisation meeting into a contest of conviction rather than evidence; the fix is a standing rule that no estimate is heard without a stated low and high. The fourth is importing another launch's observed lift wholesale without checking that its starting conditions — funnel stage, audience segment, market maturity — actually match the current one; the cheap check is simply listing those three conditions side by side before quoting someone else's number.

VIII. What good looks like

Ananya's finished estimate did what a good one does: it used two independent methods — a bottom-up decomposition from first principles and a top-down comparison to the Andaaz Wallet analog — and they landed close enough to each other to be trustworthy. She named the one assumption the whole projection hinged on, the size of the truly affected population, and showed the room exactly how much the answer moved when that single number changed. She paired the range, ₹2.11 crore to ₹9.58 crore in annual net revenue depending on that assumption, against the save-for-later feature's own range of roughly ₹0.4 crore to ₹1.3 crore, built the same way. And she did not stop at the estimate: she proposed the specific three-week holdout test that would tell the team, once the feature shipped, whether reality had landed inside her stated range — turning the estimate from a one-time pitch into the first half of a measurement loop that would close after launch.

IX. The decision, and two questions

The room chose one-tap checkout. Even its pessimistic case, ₹2.11 crore, beat save-for-later's optimistic case, and the underlying assumption — that only first-time-this-month shoppers felt the friction — was checkable within days of shipping, rather than resting on faith for a quarter. Ananya's stated next step for the team was to pair this discipline with the retention and cohort analysis needed to instrument the holdout properly, since an estimate only earns its keep once it is checked against what the funnel actually does after the build. Two questions are worth sitting with afterward: which single input in your own next estimate are you least sure of, and what would you actually do differently if that number turned out to be half of what you assumed? And is the projected return, however carefully built, worth six weeks of a team's time compared with the next best thing they could have built instead?

Bandhini: Three Features and One Festive Season

Bengaluru, July 2026. Six engineer-weeks of spare capacity, three proposals, one code freeze, and a question nobody in the room had yet answered: how much would any of them actually be worth?

1. The room on Sarjapur Road

At 3.40 on the afternoon of Wednesday 22 July 2026, Ananya Deshmukh closed her laptop in the middle of her own meeting. She was Senior Product Manager for the shopping experience at Bandhini, and the meeting — the third on this subject in nine days — had just circled back to where the previous two had ended. Three proposals were on the table. The engineering manager had capacity for one substantial build or two small ones before the festive code freeze on 5 September. Each proposal had a sponsor who wanted it, and the sponsors were now arguing about taste.

Ananya's deadline was Friday 31 July. That was when the festive release plan went to Bandhini's founder-CEO and, more consequentially, to the operations head who had to staff a warehouse in Bhiwandi for the Navratri-to-Diwali peak. What she needed by Friday was not a preference. It was a number for each proposal that the three sponsors would accept as fairly constructed even if they disagreed with the conclusion.

2. Bandhini

Bandhini was founded in 2019 in Jaipur by a brother and sister who had grown up in their family's block-printing business and thought the category deserved better photography than it was getting. It sold women's ethnic and fusion wear — kurta sets, co-ords, lightly embroidered festive pieces — at price points between ₹1,400 and ₹6,500, sitting above Meesho and below the designer end. The head office had moved to Bengaluru in 2022. By mid-2026 the company was doing about ₹340 crore of annualised gross merchandise value, of which roughly 46 per cent came through its own app and website and the rest through Myntra, Ajio and Nykaa Fashion. Established brands like W and Biba held the department-store shelf; Fabindia held the handloom conversation; Bandhini's claim was fit and colour.

The app had 820,000 monthly active users. Payments ran through Razorpay, with UPI accounting for just over half of prepaid orders and cash-on-delivery still taking 34 per cent of volume — a figure the finance team had been trying to reduce for two years, because a COD order cost more to serve and was far likelier to be refused at the door.

The team was not in one place. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune. Lena Brandt, the design lead, worked from Berlin and was awake for exactly two hours of the Indian afternoon. Rhea Mathew, the data scientist, was in Toronto, which meant her queries arrived while Bengaluru slept and her questions arrived while Bengaluru was in stand-up. Sameer Kapadia ran the small wholesale and diaspora business from New Jersey, and Bandhini's largest single overseas account was Mehfil Boutiques, a six-store chain in Dubai that bought festive collections in bulk and had begun asking whether Bandhini could ship gift orders directly to its customers' relatives in India.

3. The situation

The proximate cause of the three proposals was a number Rhea had put in a Toronto-timestamped memo in June: Bandhini's app converted app-opener to delivered and kept order at 3.3 per cent, while its own customer research suggested intent was far higher than that. Ananya had asked her to build the full funnel, from app open through to the order that survived returns. Exhibit 1 is what came back.

Rhea's second finding, in Exhibit 2, was less expected. Bandhini's return rate was 29.8 per cent of orders placed, and the single largest reason code was size and fit. Reverse logistics cost ₹210 per returned unit and refurbishment a further ₹95; a returned festive piece often could not be resold at full price at all. In contribution terms, a return did not merely cancel a sale — it destroyed roughly ₹305 on top of it.

The three proposals landed in the fortnight that followed, each aimed at a different part of Exhibit 1, and each with a sponsor who had read the memo selectively.

4. The people

Ananya Deshmukh, Senior PM, Bengaluru. Two years at Bandhini, five before that at a payments company. She was measured on kept-order contribution, not on conversion, a distinction she had asked for herself at the last appraisal cycle and was now slightly regretting.

Lena Brandt, Design Lead, Berlin. Sponsor of the size-confidence proposal. Lena had run fit interviews over video with 22 customers in Indore, Kochi and Lucknow and had come away convinced that women were abandoning at the size step because Bandhini's size chart contradicted the marketplaces' charts for the same garment. She wanted a two-question fit quiz plus a recommendation drawn from the customer's own past orders.

Vikram Nair, Engineering Manager, Pune. Sponsor of one-tap checkout with a saved UPI mandate and a prepaid nudge. His argument was practical: four engineer-weeks, no design dependency on Berlin, and a direct hit on the step where Bandhini lost the most rupees per user. He had also, privately, been told by finance that reducing COD share was a board-level goal.

Sameer Kapadia, Head of International, New Jersey. Sponsor of the festive gifting flow — gift wrap, a message card, scheduled delivery and a "send to a relative in India" address book. Mehfil Boutiques in Dubai had asked for it, and Sameer believed the diaspora gifting market around Diwali was worth far more than anyone in Bengaluru credited. He had no funnel data at all, because the flow did not exist.

Rhea Mathew, Data Scientist, Toronto. No proposal of her own. Her position was that two of the three proposals could be sized from existing data and one could not, and that this asymmetry should be made explicit rather than smoothed over.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the funnel Rhea built for June 2026, on the app only, counting distinct users within a seven-day window. Ananya's instruction had been that it must not stop at the order; it must end at the order that survived the return window, because that was the only event that put money in the company.

6. The options

Option A — size confidence. A two-question fit quiz plus a recommendation from the customer's own purchase history, shown at the size step and repeated on the cart page. Lena estimated eight engineer-weeks with her design time overlapping. Its claim is double: lift the size-selection step, where 306,000 users a month are lost, and reduce the 4,010 monthly fit returns. Its cost is that it exceeds the available capacity unless something is cut, and that it depends on Berlin design reviews at two in the morning Pune time.

Option B — one-tap checkout and prepaid nudge. Saved UPI mandate, a single-screen checkout, and a small incentive for choosing prepaid. Four engineer-weeks, no Berlin dependency, aimed squarely at the checkout-started to order-placed step where 22,500 users a month are lost, and secondarily at the 2,610 COD refusals. Its cost is that the prepaid incentive is a real discount that comes out of contribution, and that Vikram's own estimate of the conversion lift was, by his admission, "a feel".

Option C — festive gifting flow. Gift wrap, message card, scheduled delivery and a relative's address book, plus a Dubai-facing landing page for Mehfil Boutiques' customers. Eleven engineer-weeks. Its upside is a market Bandhini does not serve at all today, and a strategic relationship with its largest overseas account. Its cost is that it cannot be sized from Exhibit 1, because none of its users are in Exhibit 1, and that it would consume the entire festive window.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what is the maximum amount of money each of the three options could possibly be worth in a month — the ceiling, assuming the feature works perfectly for everyone it can reach?

2. For Option A, what fraction of the 306,000 users lost at the size step can a fit quiz plausibly reach, and what evidence in the case bears on that question? What would you need to query to find out?

3. Option C cannot be sized from the existing funnel. Does that make it a worse bet than A or B, or only a differently-risked one? How would you decide about it?

4. It is Friday 31 July. What do you put in the plan, and what single sentence do you write next to each number so that Lena, Vikram and Sameer accept the arithmetic even if they dislike the answer?

8. A note for the learner

This case is about sizing a change before it exists. The technique is a chain of multiplications: reach × addressable loss × capture rate × downstream survival × value per unit. The discipline is to build it the same way for every option, so that three proposals with three sponsors become three comparable quantities.

Start with ceilings, because they are the only honest numbers available and they kill weak options quickly. Option B's ceiling is bounded by the 22,500 users lost at checkout: recovering all of them, at a 70.2 per cent survival rate and ₹640 of contribution, would be about ₹1.01 crore a month, plus up to ₹6.7 lakh of avoided COD refusals. That ceiling is enormous, which tells you the step matters — but the capture rate for a checkout redesign on a product that already has UPI is historically small, in the low single digits of relative lift.

Option A is the interesting one because it earns money in two places. On the funnel side, its reach is not 306,000: a fit quiz can only help users who reach the size step and are uncertain, and a past-purchase recommendation only helps repeat customers. If, say, 40 per cent of the loss at that step is fit-uncertainty rather than browsing, the addressable loss is roughly 122,000, and a 10 per cent capture gives about 12,200 extra size selections — which then must survive 71.8 per cent, 41.2 per cent, 63.1 per cent and 70.2 per cent to become kept orders, a combined 13.1 per cent, or about 1,600 orders and ₹10.2 lakh of contribution. On the returns side, the arithmetic is much tighter, because Exhibit 2 gives the number directly: 4,010 fit returns a month, each destroying ₹305 of logistics cost and ₹640 of contribution, or ₹37.9 lakh in total. A 25 per cent reduction is worth about ₹9.5 lakh a month with far less guesswork in the chain, because reach there is 100 per cent of returners and the causal story is short.

Option C has no denominator. Sameer's market may be large, but nothing in the case sizes it, and eleven engineer-weeks against an unsized opportunity in the only window that matters is a poor use of the last capacity before a freeze.

One defensible path. Ship Option A, de-scoped to fit the six weeks: the past-purchase size recommendation and a fit-confidence indicator on the product page, without the full quiz, plus the size-related copy fix Lena's interviews pointed to. Ship Option B's saved-UPI change only if it can be done in the remaining fortnight without the discount, since the discount consumes the contribution the feature is meant to create. Give Option C two weeks of Rhea's time after the freeze to size the diaspora gifting opportunity properly — a landing page test run against Mehfil's own customer list would produce a reach number by December, in time for the spring planning round.

The reasoning behind that path is not that Option A has the biggest ceiling — it does not; Option B does. It is that Option A's estimate rests on the fewest guesses. Its returns benefit is measured against a known population with a known cost, while Option B's benefit rests entirely on a capture rate that Vikram himself called a feel. When two options are of similar expected size, prefer the one whose number you could defend line by line, and spend the difference in confidence on learning about the third.
